A reversible reaction proceeds in both directions because its products can react to form the reactants under suitable conditions. An irreversible reaction proceeds effectively in only one direction because the reverse reaction does not occur appreciably.
Combustion reactions are generally irreversible because they form stable products that do not readily react to reform the fuel and oxygen.
A reversible reaction can proceed in both forward and backward directions; an irreversible reaction proceeds effectively in one direction under the stated conditions.
These phase changes are reversible: ice melts and water freezes; liquid water evaporates and water vapour condenses.

As equilibrium is approached, the forward reaction rate decreases and the backward reaction rate increases. At equilibrium, the two rates are equal.
A catalyst increases both reaction rates, allowing equilibrium to be reached sooner, but it does not change the equilibrium position or yield.
